html:
The Kedukan Bukit inscription is a small stone found near Palembang in South Sumatra, dated 683 CE. It is the oldest surviving text in Old Malay and one of the founding records of Srivijaya, the trading empire of the Strait of Malacca.

It is written in the Pallava script of south India. It tells how a ruler called Dapunta Hyang set out by boat on a sacred journey with a large army, won victories, and founded a settlement that brought wealth and power. The date is given in the Saka era as the year 605, and its numerals include one of the oldest known uses of a written zero, alongside a Khmer inscription from the same year.

A Dutchman found the stone in 1920 on the bank of a tributary of the Musi River, and it is now in the National Museum in Jakarta. A few years before it was carved, the Chinese monk Yijing had stopped at Srivijaya to study Sanskrit; see Yijing at Srivijaya.
